'''whew<sup>1</sup>''' (hwū), ''v. i.'' [< ''whew''<sup>1</sup>, ''interj.''] To utter the interjection whew or a sound like it; whistle with a shrill pipe, as a plover or duck.

{{smaller block|I had often been wondering how they [the plovers] staid sae lang on the heights that year, for I heard them aye ''whewing'' e’en an’ morn.
{{right|''Hogg,'' Brownie, iii.}}}}

'''whew<sup>2</sup>''' (hwū), ''v. i.'' [Origin obscure.] '''1.''' To fly hastily; make great speed. Also ''whiew. Brockett; Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''2.''' To hurry or bustle about; work tempestuously. [New Eng.]

{{smaller block|Her father . . . had married a smart second wife “to look after matters.” . . . Nothing ever got ahead of her; she ''whewed'' round; when she was ''whewing'' she neither wanted Bel to hinder nor help.
{{right|''Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney,'' The Other Girls, vii. 112.}}}}

'''whew<sup>2</sup>''' (hwū), ''n.'' [< ''whew''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] A sudden vanishing away. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''whew-duck''' (hwū′duk), ''n.'' [< ''whew''<sup>1</sup> + ''duck;'' cf. ''whewer.''] The pandle-whew, whewer, or widgeon, ''Mareca penelope,'' among whose names are ''canard siffleur'' and ''Anas fistularis.'' [Local, British.]

{{smaller block|In some parts of England it [the widgeon] is . . . called the ''Whew-duck'' and Whewer.
{{right|''Yarrell,'' British Birds (4th ed.), IV. 400. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

¶
'''whey<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''quey''.
{{smaller block|5 ''wheyes'' (4 years old), £6.
{{right|''H. Hall'', Society in Elizabethan Age, App. I.}}}}

'''whey-beard''' (hwā′bērd), ''n.'' The whitethroat, ''Sylvia cinerea. Macgillivray; Montagu.'' See cut under ''whitethroat.'' [Local, British.]

'''wheyey''' (hwā′i), ''a.'' [< ''whey''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ey'' for ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Partaking of the nature of whey; containing or resembling whey. ''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 43.

'''whey-face''' (hwā′fās), ''n.'' [< ''whey''<sup>1</sup> + ''face''<sup>1</sup>.] A face white or pale, as from fear; also, a person having a white or pale face, or looking pale from fright.
{{smaller block|<poem>Go, prick thy face, and over-red thy fear.
. . . What soldiers, ''whey-face?''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 3. 17.}}}}

'''whey-faced''' (hwā′fāst), ''a.'' [< ''whey''<sup>1</sup> + ''face''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''cream-faced.''] Having a white or pale face; pallid.
{{smaller block|<poem>All this You made me quit, to follow
That sneaking, ''Whey-fac’d'' God Apollo.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', To Fleetwood Shephard (1689).}}}}

'''wheyish''' (hwā′ish), ''a.'' [< ''whey''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Having the qualities of whey; thin; watery.
{{smaller block|If it be fresh and sweet butter; but say it be sour and ''wheyish?'' {{right|''B. Jonson'', Staple of News, ii. 1.}}
A diet of Asses or other ''Wheyish'' Milk.
{{right|''G. Harvey'', Vanities of Philosophy and Physick (ed. 1702), xi.}}}}

'''wheyishness''' (hwā′ish-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being wheyish. ''Southey.'' (''Worcester''.)

'''whey-whig''' (hwā′hwig), ''n.'' A pleasant and sharp beverage, made by infusing mint or sage in buttermilk-whey. ''Halliwell.''

'''whey-worm''', ''n.'' See ''whay-worm.''

'''whf.''' An abbreviation of ''wharf.''

'''which'''<sup>1</sup> (hwich), ''pron.'' [< ME. ''which, whuch, hwuch'' (also unassibilated ''hwic''), a reduced form, with loss of orig. ''l'', of *''whilch, whulch, wilche, hwilch, wulch, hwulch'', assibilated forms of ''whilk, whilc, whulc, hwulc'' (> Sc. ''whilk, quhilk''), < AS. ''hwilc, hwylc, hwelc'' = OS. ''hwilīk'' = OFries. ''hwelīk, hwelk, hwek'' = D. ''welk'' = MLG. LG. ''welk'' = OHG. ''hwelīh, welīh, wielīh, welich, welch,'' MHG. ''welch, welich,'' G. ''welche,'' which, = Icel. ''hvīlīkr,'' of what kind, = Sw. Dan. ''hvilken,'' m., ''hvilket,'' neut., = Goth. ''hweileiks,'' which; < ''hwa,'' the stem of AS. ''hwā,'' etc., who, + AS. ''-līc,'' etc., a formative seen also in ''such'' (which is closely parallel phonetically to ''which''), ''each,'' etc.] '''A.''' ''interrog.'' What one of a certain implied number or set? indicating a general knowledge of a certain group of individuals, and seeking for a selection of one or more from that number: thus, ''which'' do you want? implying a limitation which is absent from the question ''what'' do you want?
{{smaller block|Many good works have I shewed you from my Father; for ''which'' of those works do ye stone me? {{right|John x. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Who is it that says most? ''which'' can say more
Than this rich praise, that you alone are you?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lxxxiv.}}}}
{{smaller block|Are any of these charges admitted to be true by the friends of the Administration, and, if any, ''which''?
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Senate, June 27, 1834.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|whether|6896|which}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|Sometimes the correlative clause is formed simply by a particle of negation.}}

{{smaller block|''Whether'' one Nym . . . had the chain ''or'' no.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iv. 5. 33.}}}}

{{smaller block|This obscure thorn-eater of malice and detraction, as well as of Quodlibets and Sophisms, knowes not ''whether'' it were illegall ''or'' not. {{right|''Milton'', An Apology, etc.}}}}

{{smaller block|His [Solomon’s] case is left disputable to this day, ''whether'' he ever recovered by repentance ''or'' no.
{{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, II. iii.}}}}

{{smaller block|''Whether'' we are in Danger ''or'' no at present, ’twere Presumption in me to judge. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. vi. 11.}}}}

<poem>To that frere wyll I go,
And bring him to you,
''Whether'' he wyl ''or'' no.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Playe of Robyn Hode'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 421).}}}}

'''2.''' Introducing a single alternative, the other being implied: as, I do not know ''whether'' he is yet gone [or not].

{{smaller block|God woot ''wher'' he was like a manly knyghte.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 1263.}}}}

{{smaller block|You shall demand of him ''whether'' one Captain Dumain be i’ the camp. {{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, iv. 3. 199.}}}}

{{smaller block|These are but winds and flaws to try the floting vessell of our faith ''whether'' it be stanch and sayl well.
{{right|''Milton'', Church-Government, i. 7.}}}}

{{smaller block|These dark doctrines and puzzling passages were inserted to be the test of ingenuous, of sincere and well-disposed minds: to see, ''whether'', when we were once satisfied that a book came from God, we would acquiesce in every thing contained in it. {{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, II. ix.}}}}

'''Whether or no.''' See ''no''<sup>1</sup>.

{{smaller block|He would be as likely to believe me guilty as not. . . . What would he do, ''whether or no?''
{{right|''Dickens'', Bleak House, lii.}}}}

'''whether'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''adv.'' An obsolete form of ''whither''.

'''whethering''' (hweᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-ing), ''n.''   [Origin obscure.]   The retention of the afterbirth in cows.   ''Gardner.''

'''whethersoᵗ''' (hweᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-sō), ''indef. pron.''   [ME.; < ''whether''<sup>1</sup> + ''so''<sup>1</sup>.]   Whichever of two, or of the two.
{{smaller block|Warne alle the compaignye that longen to this fraternite, man and woman, that is with-inne the toune, to come to the exequies of hym or of hir that is deede, ''whethir-so'' it be.
{{right|''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 74.}}}}

'''whetile''' (hwē′til), ''n.''   [Imitative; cf. ''yaffle.'']   The green woodpecker, ''Gecinus viridis.'' See cut under ''popinjay.''

'''whet-slate''' (hwet′slāt), ''n.'' A very fine-grained hard silicious rock, suitable for making whetstones and hones. Also called ''novaculite'' and ''honestone.''

'''whetstone''' (hwet′stōn), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''whestone''; < ME. ''whetston, wetston, watston, weston,'' < AS. ''hwetstān'' (= MD. ''wetsteen'' = MLG. ''wettestēn, wetstēn'' = OHG. ''wezzistein,'' MHG. ''wetzestein,'' G. ''wetzstein''), a whetstone, < ''hwettan,'' whet, + ''stan,'' stone.]   '''1.''' A stone for sharpening cutlery or tools by friction. {{smaller|Whetstones are made of various kinds of stone, the finer kinds being a silicious slate, and when used are moistened with oil or water.}}
{{smaller block|Diligence is to the understanding as the ''whetstone'' to the razor.
{{right|''South.''}}}}
{{smaller block|''Whetstones'' or scythestones used to be made solely by hand in large quantities at stone quarries in Derbyshire. {{right|''N. and Q.'', 7th ser., XI. 173.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, that which sharpens, stimulates, or incites the faculties or appetites.

{{smaller block|I assure you, there is no such ''whetstone'' to sharpen a good witte and encourage a will to learninge as is praise.
{{right|''Ascham'', The Scholemaster, p. 26.}}}}
<poem>Let them read Shakespeare’s sonnets, taking thence
A ''whetstone'' for their dull intelligence.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shelley'', To his Genius.}}}}

'''To give, deserve, or win the whetstone†''', old phrases in which a whetstone appears as the proverbial prize for lying. Confirmed liars or slanderers were sometimes publicly exhibited with a whetstone fastened to them. Compare the following allusions.

{{smaller block|If Mother Hubbard, in the vein of Chaucer, happened to tell one canicular tale, father Elderton and his son Greene, in the vein of Skelton, or Scoggin, will counterfeit an hundred dogged fables, libels, calumnies, slanders, ''lies for the whetstone'', what not. {{right|''G. Harvey'', Four Letters.}}}}
<poem>The ''whetstone'' is a knave that all men know,
Yet many on him doe much cost bestowe:
Hee’s us’d almost in every shoppe, but whye?
An edge must needs be set on every lye.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|Quoted in ''Chamber’s Book of Days'', II. 45.}}}}

{{smaller block|This will explain a smart repartee of Sir Francis Bacon’s before King James, to whom Sir Kenelm Digby was relating that he had seen the true philosopher’s stone in the possession of a hermit in Italy, and when the king was very curious to understand what sort of stone it was, and Sir Kenelm much puzzled in describing it, Sir Fra. Bacon interposed, and said, “Perhaps it was a ''whetstone''.”
{{right|''Z. Grey''.}}}}

'''whetstone-slate''' (hwet′stōn-slāt), ''n.'' Same as ''whet-slate''.

'''whetten†''' (hwet′n), ''v. t.''   [< ''whet'' + ''-en''<sup>1</sup>.]   To whet. [Rare.]

<poem>My mynd was greedelye ''whetned''
Too parle with the Regent.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Stanihurst'', Æneid, iii.}}}}

'''whetter''' (hwet′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''whet'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who or that which whets or sharpens.
{{smaller block|Love, like other sweet things, is no ''whetter'' of the stomach.
{{right|''Fielding'', Joseph Andrews. (''Latham.'')}}}}
'''2†.''' Specifically, one who indulges in whets or drams; a dram-drinker; a tippler.
{{smaller block|There are in and about the Royal-Exchange a sort of people commonly known by the name of ''Whetters'', who drink themselves into an intermediate state of being neither drunk nor sober before the hours of Exchange or business.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 138.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''Whetter'' is obliged to refresh himself every moment with a liquor, as the Snuff-taker with a powder.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 141.}}}}

'''wheugh,''' ''interj.'' A variant of ''whew''<sup>1</sup>.

'''whew'''<sup>1</sup> (hwū), ''interj.''   [Sometimes also ''wheugh'', formerly also ''whu''; an exclamation in imitation of whistling; cf. Icel. ''hviss!'' Cf. ''whoot'' for ''hoot''.]   An exclamation, uttered with a whistling sound, expressing astonishment or dismay.
{{smaller block|<poem>In a cold morning, ''whu'' — at a lord’s gate,
How you have let the porter let me wait!</poem>
{{right|''Vanbrugh'', Confederacy, Prol.}}}}
{{smaller block|He swears by the Rood. ''Whew!''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Queen Mary, i. 1.}}}}

'''whew'''<sup>1</sup> (hwū), ''n.''   [Sometimes also ''wheugh'', formerly also ''whue''; < ''whew''<sup>1</sup>, ''interj.'' or ''v.'']   '''1.''' A whistling sound, usually noting astonishment.
{{smaller block|<poem>The fryer set his fist to his mouth,
And whuted ''whues'' three.</poem>
{{right|''Robin Hood and the Curtall Fryer'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 276).}}}}
{{smaller block|Behind them lay two long, low, ugly-looking craft, at sight of which Yeo gave a long ''wheugh''.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Westward Ho, xix.}}}}
{{smaller block|Lepel suppressed a ''whew.''
{{right|''Hannay,'' Singleton Fontenoy, ix.}}}}
'''2.''' Same as ''whewer.''

{{smaller block|Wigeon (French Vigeon, from the Latin Vipio), also called locally “Whewer” and “''Whew''” (names imitative of the whistling call-note of the male).
{{right|''A. Newton,'' Encyc. Brit., XXIV. 561.}}}}

{{right|''Hogg,'' Brownie, iii.}}}}

'''whew-duck''' (hwū′duk), ''n.''   [< ''whew''<sup>1</sup> + ''duck;'' cf. ''whewer.'']   The pandle-whew, whewer, or widgeon, ''Mareca penelope,'' among whose names are ''canard siffleur'' and ''Anas fistularis.'' [Local, British.]

'''whewellite''' (hwū′el-īt), ''n.''   [Named after W. ''Whewell'', master of Trinity College, Cambridge.]   Native calcium oxalate, a rare mineral occurring in monoclinic crystals, colorless or white with brilliant luster.

'''whewer''' (hwū′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''whew''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   The whew-duck. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|In Norfolk, according to Ray, ''whewers.''
{{right|''C. Swainson'', Brit. Birds (1885), p. 155.}}}}

'''whey'''<sup>1</sup> (hwā), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''whay;'' also dial. ''whig;'' < ME. ''whey'', ''whei'', ''hwei'', < AS. ''hwǣg'' = Fries. ''weye'' = MD. ''wey'', D. ''wei'', also MD. ''huy'', ''hoy'', ''hui'' = LG. ''wey'', ''waje'', ''hei'', ''heu'', whey; root unknown. Cf. W. ''chwig'', whey fermented with sour herbs; ''chwig'', sour, fermented.]   The serum of milk; that part of milk which remains fluid after the proteids have been coagulated by rennet as in cheese-making, or by an acid as in the natural souring of milk. {{smaller|Whey is often mixed with wine, or flavored with herbs, spices, etc., and used as a cooling beverage.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The pined Fisher or poor-Daiery-Renter
That liues of ''whay'', for forfeiting Indenture.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Down to the milke-house, and drank three glasses of ''whey.''
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, II. 398.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Alum whey''', the whey formed in the coagulation of milk by powdered alum.—'''Whey cure''', the treatment of certain diseases by means of the internal administration of quantities of whey, sometimes combined with baths in the same liquid. This “cure” is usually practised in connection with drinking and bathing in mineral waters at European spas.—'''Wine whey.''' See ''wine.''}}

'''whey<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''quey''.
{{smaller block|5 ''wheyes'' (4 years old), £6.
{{right|''H. Hall'', Society in Elizabethan Age, App. I.}}}}

'''wheyey''' (hwā′i), ''a.''   [< ''whey''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ey'' for ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Partaking of the nature of whey; containing or resembling whey.   ''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 43.

'''whey-face''' (hwā′fās), ''n.''   [< ''whey''<sup>1</sup> + ''face''<sup>1</sup>.]   A face white or pale, as from fear; also, a person having a white or pale face, or looking pale from fright.
{{smaller block|<poem>Go, prick thy face, and over-red thy fear.
. . . What soldiers, ''whey-face?''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 3. 17.}}}}

'''whey-faced''' (hwā′fāst), ''a.''   [< ''whey''<sup>1</sup> + ''face''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>. Cf. ''cream-faced.'']   Having a white or pale face; pallid.
{{smaller block|<poem>All this You made me quit, to follow
That sneaking, ''Whey-fac’d'' God Apollo.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', To Fleetwood Shephard (1689).}}}}

'''wheyish''' (hwā′ish), ''a.''   [< ''whey''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Having the qualities of whey; thin; watery.
{{smaller block|If it be fresh and sweet butter; but say it be sour and ''wheyish?'' {{right|''B. Jonson'', Staple of News, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|A diet of Asses or other ''Wheyish'' Milk.
{{right|''G. Harvey'', Vanities of Philosophy and Physick (ed. 1702), xi.}}}}

'''wheyishness''' (hwā′ish-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being wheyish.   ''Southey.'' (''Worcester''.)

'''whey-whig''' (hwā′hwig), ''n.'' A pleasant and sharp beverage, made by infusing mint or sage in buttermilk-whey.   ''Halliwell.''

'''whey-worm''', ''n.'' See ''whay-worm.''

'''whf.''' An abbreviation of ''wharf.''

'''which'''<sup>1</sup> (hwich), ''pron.''   [< ME. ''which, whuch, hwuch'' (also unassibilated ''hwic''), a reduced form, with loss of orig. ''l'', of *''whilch, whulch, wilche, hwilch, wulch, hwulch'', assibilated forms of ''whilk, whilc, whulc, hwulc'' (> Sc. ''whilk, quhilk''), < AS. ''hwilc, hwylc, hwelc'' = OS. ''hwilīk'' = OFries. ''hwelīk, hwelk, hwek'' = D. ''welk'' = MLG. LG. ''welk'' = OHG. ''hwelīh, welīh, wielīh, welich, welch,'' MHG. ''welch, welich,'' G. ''welche,'' which, = Icel. ''hvīlīkr,'' of what kind, = Sw. Dan. ''hvilken,'' m., ''hvilket,'' neut., = Goth. ''hweileiks,'' which; < ''hwa,'' the stem of AS. ''hwā,'' etc., who, + AS. ''-līc,'' etc., a formative seen also in ''such'' (which is closely parallel phonetically to ''which''), ''each,'' etc.]   '''A.''' ''interrog.'' What one of a certain implied number or set? indicating a general knowledge of a certain group of individuals, and seeking for a selection of one or more from that number: thus, ''which'' do you want? implying a limitation which is absent from the question ''what'' do you want?
{{smaller block|Many good works have I shewed you from my Father; for ''which'' of those works do ye stone me? {{right|John x. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Who is it that says most? ''which'' can say more
Than this rich praise, that you alone are you?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, lxxxiv.}}}}
{{smaller block|Are any of these charges admitted to be true by the friends of the Administration, and, if any, ''which''?
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Senate, June 27, 1834.}}}}

{{smaller block|But ''which'' is it to be? Fight or make friends? “Why,” says he, “I think it will be the best manner to spin a coin for it.” {{right|''R. L. Stevenson'', Master of Ballantrae, ii.}}}}
{{smaller|Used adjectively, with a selective and interrogative force, to limit a noun.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Cost.'' From my lord to my lady.
''Prin.'' From ''which'' lord to ''which'' lady?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., iv. 1. 105.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Me miserable! ''which'' way shall I fly
Infinite wrath and infinite despair?</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 73.}}}}
{{smaller|In an old exclamatory use, what!}}
{{smaller block|<poem>“Lo!” seith holy letterure, “''whiche'' lordes beth this shrewes [are these wretches]!”
Thilke that god moste gyueth, leste good thei deleth.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), x. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|Kay the stiward . . . dide as a noble knyght; ffor the thre Princes seide, “Mercy god, ''whiche'' a stiward is this!” {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 661.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Which is which?''' which is the one, which the other? a common phrase implying inability to distinguish between two or more things. Used relatively as well as interrogatively: see the quotation.}}
{{smaller block|The whole mass of buildings is jammed together in a manner that from certain points of view makes it far from apparent ''which'' feature ''is which.'' {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 159.}}}}

'''B.''' ''rel.'' '''1.''' As a simple relative pronoun: (''a'') Who or whom. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Now that I see my lady bright
''Which'' I have loved with al my might.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 478.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The yonger sone ser Abell was his name,
''Whiche'' of his enmys had but litill drede.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1922.}}}}
{{smaller block|Our Father ''which'' art in heaven. {{right|Mat. vi. 9.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
